claim: AITC (allyl isothiocyanate; mustard oil) and menthol represent two distinct types of ligands at the mammalian cold sensor TRPM8.
source: Here we show that AITC (allyl isothiocyanate; mustard oil) and menthol represent two distinct types of ligands at the mammalian cold sensor TRPM8.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a main finding of the study.

claim: AITC acts by destabilizing the closed channel relative to the transition state.
source: Kinetic analysis of channel gating revealed that AITC acts by destabilizing the closed channel, whereas menthol stabilizes the open channel, relative to the transition state.
evidence: This is stated as a result from kinetic analysis of channel gating.

claim: Menthol stabilizes the open channel relative to the transition state.
source: Kinetic analysis of channel gating revealed that AITC acts by destabilizing the closed channel, whereas menthol stabilizes the open channel, relative to the transition state.
evidence: This is stated as a result from kinetic analysis of channel gating.

claim: Type I agonists (menthol-like) stabilize the open channel.
source: Based on these differences, we classify agonists as either type I (menthol-like) or type II (AITC-like), and provide a kinetic model that faithfully reproduces their differential effects.
evidence: The classification is based on kinetic analysis and modeling of agonist effects.

claim: Type II agonists (AITC-like) destabilize the closed channel.
source: Based on these differences, we classify agonists as either type I (menthol-like) or type II (AITC-like), and provide a kinetic model that faithfully reproduces their differential effects.
evidence: The classification is based on kinetic analysis and modeling of agonist effects.

claim: Type I and type II agonists have a distinct impact on TRPM8 currents in excitable cells.
source: We further demonstrate that type I and type II agonists have a distinct impact on TRPM8 currents and TRPM8-mediated calcium signals in excitable cells.
evidence: This is stated as a demonstrated finding in the abstract.

claim: Type I and type II agonists have a distinct impact on TRPM8-mediated calcium signals in excitable cells.
source: We further demonstrate that type I and type II agonists have a distinct impact on TRPM8 currents and TRPM8-mediated calcium signals in excitable cells.
evidence: This is stated as a demonstrated finding in the abstract.

claim: Several members of the TRP superfamily of cation channels act as polymodal molecular sensors of both temperature and a variety of endogenous and exogenous chemicals.
source: Within the somatosensory system, several members of the TRP superfamily of cation channels act as polymodal molecular sensors of both temperature, and a variety of endogenous and exogenous chemicals, including a plethora of plant-derived compounds (Clapham, 2003; Tominaga et al., 1998; Voets et al., 2005; Vriens et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Capsaicin acts as a selective agonist of the heat-activated TRPV1.
source: such as the burning heat evoked by capsaicin (the pungent substance in hot peppers), which acts as a selective agonist of the heat-activated TRPV1 (Caterina et al., 1997)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Menthol activates the cold sensor TRPM8.
source: and the cool sensation evoked by menthol (the cooling compound in mint plants), due to activation of the cold sensor TRPM8 (McKemy et al., 2002; Peier et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: AITC is responsible for the characteristic oral sensations experienced upon eating Dijon mustard or wasabi.
source: AITC is responsible for the characteristic oral sensations that one experiences upon eating Dijon mustard or wasabi, which contain between 5–30 mM of AITC (Uematsu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Dijon mustard and wasabi contain between 5–30 mM of AITC.
source: AITC is responsible for the characteristic oral sensations that one experiences upon eating Dijon mustard or wasabi, which contain between 5–30 mM of AITC (Uematsu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: AITC activates TRPA1 in nociceptor neurons.
source: Whereas earlier work has firmly established that AITC activates TRPA1 and TRPV1 in nociceptor neurons, approximately 10% of dorsal root ganglion neurons remained AITC-responsive after combined genetic deletion these two TRP channels (Bandell et al., 2004; Bautista et al., 2006; Everaerts et al., 2011; Jordt et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established by earlier work with citations.

claim: AITC activates TRPV1 in nociceptor neurons.
source: Whereas earlier work has firmly established that AITC activates TRPA1 and TRPV1 in nociceptor neurons, approximately 10% of dorsal root ganglion neurons remained AITC-responsive after combined genetic deletion these two TRP channels (Bandell et al., 2004; Bautista et al., 2006; Everaerts et al., 2011; Jordt et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established by earlier work with citations.

claim: Approximately 10% of dorsal root ganglion neurons remained AITC-responsive after combined genetic deletion of TRPA1 and TRPV1.
source: Whereas earlier work has firmly established that AITC activates TRPA1 and TRPV1 in nociceptor neurons, approximately 10% of dorsal root ganglion neurons remained AITC-responsive after combined genetic deletion these two TRP channels (Bandell et al., 2004; Bautista et al., 2006; Everaerts et al., 2011; Jordt et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: AITC excites a subset of somatosensory neurons via direct activation of TRPM8.
source: In this work we show that AITC excites this subset of somatosensory neurons via direct activation of TRPM8.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current work.

claim: A small fraction (9%) of TRPV1/TRPA1-deficient DRG neurons showed a rapid and reversible increase in intracellular Ca2+ in response to 3 mM AITC.
source: In line with previous work (Everaerts et al., 2011), we found that a small fraction of these TRPV1/TRPA1-deficient neurons (55 out of 578; 9% ) showed a rapid and reversible increase in intracellular Ca2+ in response to 3 mM AITC (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to a figure.

claim: 98% of AITC-responsive TRPV1/TRPA1-deficient neurons responded to menthol.
source: These AITC-responsive cells consistently responded to menthol (54 out of 55; 98%) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to figures.

claim: Responses to both AITC and menthol in TRPV1/TRPA1-deficient neurons were fully inhibited by the TRPM8 antagonist AMTB.
source: In these cells, the responses to both AITC and menthol were fully inhibited by the TRPM8 antagonist AMTB, and recovered partially upon AMTB washout (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to a figure.

claim: TRPV1- and TRPA1-independent AITC responses in DRG neurons depend on TRPM8.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that TRPV1- and TRPA1-independent AITC responses in DRG neurons depend on the cold- and menthol-sensitive channel TRPM8.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Application of AITC at concentrations ≥300 μM caused a rapid and reversible increase in TRPM8 current.
source: Application of AITC at concentrations ≥300 μM caused a rapid and reversible increase in TRPM8 current (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure.

claim: The amplitude of AITC-induced TRPM8 response increased with AITC concentration but did not saturate at the highest concentration tested (10 mM).
source: The amplitude of the response increased with AITC concentration, with relatively stronger effects at negative voltages, but did not saturate at the highest concentration tested (10 mM; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure.

claim: At 3 and 10 mM AITC, activation was followed by a gradual decay of TRPM8 current, reducing current amplitude to levels below the basal level.
source: At 3 and 10 mM AITC, activation was followed by a gradual decay of TRPM8 current, reducing current amplitude to levels below the basal level (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claim: Rapid and reversible current responses to AITC were observed in cell-free inside-out patches from human TRPM8-expressing HEK293 cells.
source: Rapid and reversible current responses to AITC were also observed in cell-free inside-out patches from human TRPM8-expressing HEK293 cells, indicating that the effect of AITC on TRPM8 is membrane-delimited (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claim: The effect of AITC on TRPM8 is membrane-delimited.
source: Rapid and reversible current responses to AITC were also observed in cell-free inside-out patches from human TRPM8-expressing HEK293 cells, indicating that the effect of AITC on TRPM8 is membrane-delimited (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the inside-out patch experiments.

claim: Application of 3 mM AITC had no detectable effect on TRPM8-mCherry fluorescence in the close vicinity of the plasma membrane.
source: As shown in Figure 2F,G, application of 3 mM AITC had no detectable effect on the TRPM8-mCherry fluorescence in the close vicinity of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claim: Trafficking does not significantly contribute to the acute agonistic effect of AITC on TRPM8.
source: Since the onset of current activation by AITC was very rapid, with maximal current achieved within ~2 s (Figure 2A,D), we can exclude a significant contribution of trafficking to the acute agonistic effect of AITC on TRPM8.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the TIRF imaging and electrophysiology experiments.

claim: AITC has little or no effect on the maximal conductance of TRPM8 at strongly depolarizing potentials.
source: Analysis of the steady-state conductances revealed that AITC has little or no effect on the maximal conductance at strongly depolarizing potentials, but shifts the voltage-dependent activation curves towards more negative voltages in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to figures.

claim: AITC shifts the voltage-dependent activation curves of TRPM8 towards more negative voltages in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Analysis of the steady-state conductances revealed that AITC has little or no effect on the maximal conductance at strongly depolarizing potentials, but shifts the voltage-dependent activation curves towards more negative voltages in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to figures.

claim: In the presence of AITC, there is a clear acceleration of the gating kinetics upon depolarization to +120 mV.
source: In the presence of AITC we observed a clear acceleration of the gating kinetics upon depolarization to +120 mV, whereas the current relaxation kinetics upon repolarization to −80 mV were not markedly altered.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: In the presence of menthol, there is a pronounced slowing of the kinetics of current relaxation, most noticeable upon repolarization to −80 mV.
source: In stark contrast, in the presence of menthol we found a pronounced slowing of the kinetics of current relaxation, most noticeable upon repolarization to −80 mV (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claim: In the absence of ligands, the time courses of TRPM8 currents at +120 and −80 mV were generally well fitted by a mono-exponential function.
source: In line with earlier work, we found that in the absence of ligands the time courses at +120 and −80 mV were generally well fitted by a mono-exponential function (Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to figures.

claim: In the presence of 3 mM AITC, the time courses of TRPM8 currents remained well fitted by a mono-exponential function.
source: In the presence of 3 mM AITC, the time courses remained well fitted by a mono-exponential function, and the accelerated kinetics were reflected in a reduction of τ+120 mV compared to control, whereas τ−80 mV was unaltered (Figure 4A,B,E).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to figures.

claim: The relaxation kinetics of TRPM8 in the presence of 30 μM menthol were consistently slower than in control and were no longer mono-exponential.
source: In contrast, the relaxation kinetics in the presence of 30 μM menthol were consistently slower than in control and were no longer mono-exponential: at least two exponential terms were required to accurately describe the current time course at +120 (τ+120 mV,fast and τ+120 mV,slow) and −80 mV (τ−80 mV,fast and τ−80 mV,slow) (Figure 4A,B,F).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to figures.

claim: Other known TRPM8 agonists, including thymol, icilin, and linalool, act in a similar manner as menthol, slowing down the kinetics of activation and deactivation.
source: Other known TRPM8 agonists, including thymol, icilin, and linalool, act in a similar manner as menthol, slowing down the kinetics of activation and deactivation, albeit less pronounced (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: Type I (menthol-like) agonists induce a slowing of the gating kinetics, most prominently observed as slowly deactivating tail currents following repolarization.
source: Type I (menthol-like) agonists induce a slowing of the gating kinetics, which is most prominently observed as slowly deactivating tail currents following repolarization
evidence: This is stated as a classification based on experimental observations.

claim: Type II (AITC-like) agonists cause an acceleration of the kinetics of channel activation upon depolarization, with little or no effect on the kinetics of deactivating tail currents.
source: whereas Type II (AITC-like) agonists cause an acceleration of the kinetics of channel activation upon depolarization, with little or no effect on the kinetics of deactivating tail currents (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a classification based on experimental observations.

claim: The characteristic slowly decaying tail currents upon repolarization in the presence of menthol indicate that menthol impedes voltage-dependent channel deactivation.
source: In particular, the characteristic slowly decaying tail currents upon repolarization in the presence of menthol indicate that menthol impedes voltage-dependent channel deactivation, which points at a stabilization of the channel in an open conformation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: Menthol stabilizes the channel in an open conformation.
source: In particular, the characteristic slowly decaying tail currents upon repolarization in the presence of menthol indicate that menthol impedes voltage-dependent channel deactivation, which points at a stabilization of the channel in an open conformation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: The faster current relaxation upon depolarization in the presence of AITC indicates that AITC accelerates voltage-dependent channel activation.
source: Oppositely, the faster current relaxation upon depolarization in the presence of AITC indicates that AITC accelerates voltage-dependent channel activation, which points at a destabilization of the channel in a closed conformation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: AITC destabilizes the channel in a closed conformation.
source: Oppositely, the faster current relaxation upon depolarization in the presence of AITC indicates that AITC accelerates voltage-dependent channel activation, which points at a destabilization of the channel in a closed conformation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: A single TRPM8 channel can bind up to four ligand molecules.
source: Moreover, based on analysis of channel chimeras with different combinations of wild type and mutated menthol binding sites, it was found that a single TRPM8 channel can bind up to four ligand molecules, each subunit having and ligand binding site with an affinity Kd (in the closed state), and that every bound ligand shifts the equilibrium between the closed and open channel by a similar extent (Janssens and Voets, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Each TRPM8 subunit has a ligand binding site with an affinity Kd in the closed state.
source: Moreover, based on analysis of channel chimeras with different combinations of wild type and mutated menthol binding sites, it was found that a single TRPM8 channel can bind up to four ligand molecules, each subunit having and ligand binding site with an affinity Kd (in the closed state), and that every bound ligand shifts the equilibrium between the closed and open channel by a similar extent (Janssens and Voets, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Every bound ligand shifts the equilibrium between the closed and open TRPM8 channel by a similar extent.
source: Moreover, based on analysis of channel chimeras with different combinations of wild type and mutated menthol binding sites, it was found that a single TRPM8 channel can bind up to four ligand molecules, each subunit having and ligand binding site with an affinity Kd (in the closed state), and that every bound ligand shifts the equilibrium between the closed and open channel by a similar extent (Janssens and Voets, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Excellent fits to the experimental data were obtained when menthol binding acts exclusively by stabilization the open state, while AITC acts by destabilization of the closed state.
source: Importantly, we obtained excellent fits to the experimental data when we set fixed that menthol binding acts exclusively by stabilization the open state, while AITC acts by destabilization of the closed state (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is stated as a result from model fitting with reference to figures.

claim: The model accurately predicts the concentration-dependent effects of AITC and menthol on TRPM8.
source: Gratifyingly, the model accurately predicts the concentration-dependent effects of AITC and menthol on TRPM8, including the mono-exponential time constants in the presence of different AITC concentrations, as well as the bi-exponential relaxation kinetics in the presence of menthol, respectively (Figure 5D,E; Figure 4E,F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result from model predictions with reference to figures.

claim: AITC represents the first example of a type II TRPM8 agonist.
source: Based on these results, we propose that AITC represents the first example of a type II TRPM8 agonist, acting primarily by destabilizing the closed channel, which contrasts to the Type I agonists, such as menthol, icilin, thymol and linalool, which primarily stabilize the open channel.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Type I agonists such as menthol, icilin, thymol and linalool primarily stabilize the open channel.
source: Based on these results, we propose that AITC represents the first example of a type II TRPM8 agonist, acting primarily by destabilizing the closed channel, which contrasts to the Type I agonists, such as menthol, icilin, thymol and linalool, which primarily stabilize the open channel.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Application of 50 μM menthol results in slower activation and deactivation kinetics of TRPM8.
source: In line with the above, application of 50 μM menthol results in slower activation and deactivation kinetics, due to the stabilization of the open state (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: Addition of 3 mM AITC in the continued presence of menthol resulted in faster activation kinetics, without affecting the time course of deactivation.
source: Addition of 3 mM AITC in the continued presence of menthol resulted in faster activation kinetics, without affecting the time course of deactivation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The combined effects of AITC and menthol are in line with the predictions of the MWC model, assuming that Type I and Type II agonists can act simultaneously and independently.
source: These results are in line with the predictions of the MWC model, assuming that Type I and Type II agonists can act simultaneously and independently, resulting in both stabilization of the open and destabilization of the closed state (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between experimental results and model predictions.

claim: At a physiological holding potential of −60 mV, 3 mM AITC and 30 µM menthol resulted in comparable steady-state inward current amplitudes.
source: Note that, at a physiological holding potential of −60 mV, these concentrations resulted in comparable steady-state inward current amplitudes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure.

claim: In response to action potential waveforms, the current in the presence of AITC mainly manifested during the upstroke phase and rapidly deactivates upon action potential repolarization.
source: In response to the action potential waveforms, the current in the presence of AITC mainly manifested during the upstroke phase, and rapidly deactivates upon action potential repolarization.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: In the presence of menthol, the peak outward current during action potentials is smaller but a more prominent inward TRPM8 current is observed during the repolarization phase.
source: In comparison, in the presence of menthol, the peak outward current is smaller but a more prominent inward TRPM8 current is observed during the repolarization phase of the action potential (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claim: Net charge influx during a 1-s train of action potential waveforms at 8 Hz is larger in the presence of menthol.
source: As illustrated in Figure 6D,E, net charge influx is larger in the presence of menthol, whereas net charge efflux is larger in the presence of AITC.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claim: Net charge efflux during a 1-s train of action potential waveforms at 8 Hz is larger in the presence of AITC.
source: As illustrated in Figure 6D,E, net charge influx is larger in the presence of menthol, whereas net charge efflux is larger in the presence of AITC.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claim: Mouse TRPM8 was rapidly activated by AITC.
source: Like its human orthologue, mouse TRPM8 was rapidly activated by AITC, and the difference in gating kinetics in the presence of AITC versus menthol was also observed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: AITC-induced current inhibition was much less pronounced in mouse TRPM8 compared to the human orthologue.
source: However, interestingly, AITC-induced current inhibition was much less pronounced in mouse TRPM8 compared to the human orthologue (Figure 7—figure supplement 2): at the end of a 60-s application of 3 mM AITC, mouse TRPM8 current amounted to 88 ± 6% (n = 8) of the peak current, compared to 21 ± 5% in the case of human TRPM8 (n = 7; p=0.00004).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The amplitudes of Ca2+ transients evoked by 60-s-long applications of 3 mM AITC were on average ~30% smaller than those evoked by 30 µM menthol in TRPA1/TRPV1-deficient mouse sensory neurons.
source: In these cells, we found that the amplitudes of Ca2+ transients evoked by a 60-s-long applications of 3 mM AITC were on average ~30% smaller than those evoked by 30 µM menthol (Figure 7A,D).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claim: The peak rate of calcium rise was consistently smaller in response to AITC than to menthol in TRPA1/TRPV1-deficient neurons.
source: Likewise, the peak rate of calcium rise, which represents a measure for the maximal inward calcium current, was consistently smaller in response to AITC than to menthol in neurons (Figure 7A,D).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claim: AITC evoked larger calcium increases and with a higher peak rate of calcium rise than menthol in HEK cells expressing mouse TRPM8.
source: Interestingly, we observed an opposite potency of the same concentrations of menthol and AITC in HEK cells expressing mouse TRPM8: AITC evoked larger calcium increases and with a higher peak rate of calcium rise than did menthol (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claim: When action potential firing in TRPA1/TRPV1-deficient sensory neurons was blocked using TTX, a similar ratio of AITC versus menthol responses as in HEK cells was found.
source: Moreover, if action potential firing in the TRPA1/TRPV1-deficient sensory neurons was blocked using tetrodotoxin (TTX; 1 μM), we found a similar ratio of AITC versus menthol responses as in HEK cells (Figure 7C,D), with AITC being slightly more potent than menthol.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to figures.

claim: Compared to Type II agonists (e.g. AITC), Type I agonists (e.g. menthol) are more potent in evoking calcium influx in excitable cells.
source: Taken together, these data provide further support for the notion that, compared to Type II agonists (e.g. AITC), Type I agonists (e.g. menthol) are more potent in evoking calcium influx in excitable cells, due to enhanced calcium influx during the prolonged inward tail currents following action potentials.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: AITC is an atypical agonist of TRPM8, with a mode of action that is fundamentally different from that of all other known TRPM8-activating stimuli.
source: While there are already numerous natural and synthetic agonists known for TRPM8 (Almaraz et al., 2014), our results demonstrate that AITC is an atypical agonist, with a mode of action that is fundamentally different from that of all other known TRPM8-activating stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study with a citation.

claim: Activation of TRPM8 by cooling or by known agonists such as menthol, thymol, linalool, icilin and halothane is associated with a slowing of the kinetics of voltage-dependent channel gating.
source: Activation of TRPM8 by cooling or by known agonists such as the natural compounds menthol, thymol and linalool, and the synthetic agonists such as icilin and halothane, is associated with a slowing of the kinetics of voltage-dependent channel gating (Vanden Abeele et al., 2013; Voets et al., 2004; Voets et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The slowing of the gating kinetics by cooling and known agonists can be explained by a stabilization of the open channel relative to the transition state.
source: This slowing of the gating kinetics can be directly explained by a stabilization of the open channel relative to the transition state, as we illustrated in this work for menthol and elsewhere for cooling (Voets et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Activation of TRPM8 by AITC resulted in an acceleration of the kinetics of voltage-dependent gating.
source: In clear contrast, activation of TRPM8 by AITC resulted in an acceleration of the kinetics of voltage-dependent gating, and we show here that this can be fully explained by a mechanism where AITC leads to a relative destabilization of the closed conformation relative to the transition state.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current work.

claim: The classification of activating ligands as either Type I or Type II may be extended to activating ligands of other voltage- and ligand-sensitive TRP channels.
source: Such classification may also be extended to activating ligands of other voltage- and ligand-sensitive TRP channels.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about broader applicability.

claim: Activation of TRPV1 by capsaicin or low pH is associated with faster activation time courses upon depolarization, classifying them as Type II ligands.
source: For instance, published current traces suggest that activation of TRPV1 by capsaicin or low pH is associated with faster activation time courses upon depolarization (Aneiros et al., 2011; Voets et al., 2004), classifying them as Type II ligands
evidence: This is stated as an inference from published data with citations.

claim: The activating effects of PIP2 or lysophosphatidic acid on TRPV1 are associated with slower activation and longer deactivating tails upon repolarization, classifying them as Type I agonists.
source: whereas the activating effects of phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) or lysophosphatidic acid are associated with slower activation and longer deactivating tails upon repolarization, classifying them a Type I agonists (Nieto-Posadas et al., 2012; Ufret-Vincenty et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from published data with citations.

claim: Type II ligands such as AITC reduce the difference Gibbs free energy between the closed state and the transition state (ΔGα†), without affecting the difference Gibbs free energy between the open state and the transition state (ΔGβ†).
source: Indeed, our results indicate that Type II ligands such as AITC reduce the difference Gibbs free energy between the closed state and the transition state (ΔGα†), without affecting the difference Gibbs free energy between the open state and the transition state (ΔGβ†).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The AITC-induced conformational change at its binding site occurs early in the gating process, prior to the main close-open transition.
source: This suggests that the AITC-induced conformational change at its binding site occurs early in the gating process, prior to the main close-open transition.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the thermodynamic analysis.

claim: Type I ligands such as menthol cause an increase in ΔGβ†, without affecting ΔGα†.
source: Oppositely, Type I ligands such as menthol cause an increase in ΔGβ†, without affecting ΔGα†.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The menthol-induced conformational change at its binding sites occurs later than the main close-open transition.
source: This indicates that the menthol-induced conformational change at its binding sites occurs later than the main close-open transition.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the thermodynamic analysis.

claim: For menthol binding to TRPM8, a kon of 0.55 μM−1s−1 was obtained.
source: For example, for menthol binding we obtained a kon of 0.55 μM−1s−1, which is well below the diffusion-limited rate (>100 μM−1s−1), and also one order of magnitude or more lower than binding rates for ligands to synaptic ligand-gated channels, such as the ionotropic receptors for glutamate (kon≈ 5 μM−1s−1) (Clements and Westbrook, 1991), ATP (kon≈ 12 μM−1s−1) (Bean, 1990) or acetylcholine (kon≈ 60 μM−1s−1) (Sine et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated as a result from kinetic fits with citations for comparison.

claim: The binding site for menthol is located in a hydrophobic domain in between the transmembrane helices.
source: Indeed, whereas binding sites for glutamate, ATP and acetylcholine are located extracellularly (Hille, 2001), directly accessible from the aqueous phase, the binding site for menthol is located in a hydrophobic domain in between the transmembrane helices (Bandell et al., 2006; Voets et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The observation that current relaxation time courses of TRPM8 in the presence of menthol become multi-exponential is a direct consequence of the slow equilibration rate of menthol with its binding site in comparison to the transition rates between closed and open channel conformations.
source: The observation that current relaxation time courses of TRPM8 in the presence of menthol become multi-exponential is then a direct consequence of the slow equilibration rate of menthol with its binding site in comparison to the transition rates between closed and open channel conformations.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: The AITC-induced TRPM8 current during a typical action potential waveform mainly manifests during the upstroke phase and rapidly deactivates upon action potential repolarization.
source: Indeed, as predicted by our model, the AITC-induced TRPM8 current during a typical action potential waveform mainly manifest during the upstroke phase, and rapidly deactivates upon action potential repolarization.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation that matches model predictions.

claim: An equipotent concentration of menthol results in less outward current but more prominent activation of inward TRPM8 current during the repolarization phase following an action potential.
source: In contrast, an equipotent concentration of menthol (i.e. a concentration of menthol provoking a similar steady-state current) results in a less outward current but more prominent activation of inward TRPM8 current during the repolarization phase following an action potential, and thus leads to more Ca2+ influx via TRPM8.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Inhibiting action potential firing using TTX has a more profound effect on menthol-induced responses than on AITC-induced responses in sensory neurons.
source: In line herewith, we found that inhibiting action potential firing using TTX has a more profound effect on menthol-induced responses than on AITC-induced responses in sensory neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: TRPM8 underlies the residual TRPA1- and TRPV1-independent responses to AITC in mouse sensory neurons.
source: Our results demonstrate that TRPM8 underlies the residual TRPA1- and TRPV1-independent responses to AITC in mouse sensory neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Activation of TRPM8 by AITC only occurred in the high micromolar to millimolar concentration range under experimental conditions.
source: Under our experimental conditions, activation of TRPM8 by AITC only occurred in the high micromolar to millimolar concentration range.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: TRPM8 is about two orders of magnitude less sensitive to AITC than TRPA1.
source: As such, TRPM8 is about two orders of magnitude less sensitive to AITC than TRPA1, for which concentrations for half-maximal activation of 5–50 µM have been reported (Bandell et al., 2004; Everaerts et al., 2011; Jordt et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with citations to prior work.

claim: TRPM8 sensitivity to AITC is comparable to TRPV1, for which a concentration for half-maximal activation of 3 mM was found at room temperature.
source: but comparable to TRPV1, for which a concentration for half-maximal activation of 3 mM was found at room temperature (Everaerts et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with a citation to prior work.

claim: AITC concentrations ≤100 µM evoke responses that are strictly TRPA1-dependent in sensory neurons.
source: These findings are in line with in vitro experiments in sensory neurons, showing that AITC concentrations ≤100 µM evoke responses that are strictly TRPA1-dependent (Bautista et al., 2006; Everaerts et al., 2011)
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Higher concentrations of AITC can evoke TRPA1-independent responses mediated by TRPV1 or TRPM8.
source: whereas higher concentrations can also evoke TRPA1-independent responses mediated by TRPV1 or TRPM8.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Experimental solutions used in in vivo AITC experiments typically contain AITC at concentrations between 10 and 100 mM.
source: In such assays, experimental solutions that are injected or topically applied typically contain AITC at concentrations between 10 and 100 mM (Bautista et al., 2006; Caterina et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Pain and inflammatory responses to AITC under experimental conditions are largely mediated by TRPA1 and TRPV1.
source: Whereas earlier studies have clearly shown that pain and inflammatory responses under such experimental conditions are largely mediated by TRPA1 and TRPV1 (Bautista et al., 2006; Everaerts et al., 2011; Kwan et al., 2006)
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: TRPM8-positive sensory nerve endings may become activated at AITC doses used in in vivo experiments.
source: our present results suggest that also TRPM8-positive sensory nerve endings may become activated at these AITC doses.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the current results.

claim: Activation of TRPM8-expressing neurons can cause analgesia in animal models of acute and chronic pain.
source: Since activation of TRPM8-expressing neurons can cause analgesia in animal models of acute and chronic pain (Liu et al., 2013; Proudfoot et al., 2006)
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: A transient increase in cold sensitivity was observed upon application of 100 mM AITC on the tongue of human volunteers.
source: In line herewith, a transient increase in cold sensitivity was observed upon application of 100 mM AITC on the tongue of human volunteers (Albin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: In voltage-gated Na+, K+ and Ca2+ channels, ligand modulators have been classified based on their distinct state-dependent effects on channel gating.
source: In voltage-gated ion Na+, K+ and Ca2+ channels, ligand modulators have since decades been classified based on their distinct state-dependent effects on channel gating (Hille, 2001)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Mechanistic insight into state-dependent effects of ligands has been key to understanding their physiological impact in neurons and cardiac cells.
source: and this mechanistic insight has been key to understanding their physiological impact in for instance neurons and cardiac cells (Sack and Sum, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: This study demonstrates for the first time the existence of two types of agonists with distinct state-dependent effects for a member of the TRP superfamily.
source: In this study, we demonstrate for the first time the existence of two types of agonists with distinct state-dependent effects for a member of the TRP superfamily, the cold-sensitive TRPM8, and provide a paradigm for their differential effects in sensory neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Establishing the state-dependent mode of action of (ant)agonists of TRP channels will be essential to clarify their physiological actions.
source: We argue that establishing the state-dependent mode of action of (ant)agonists of this and other TRP channels will be essential to clarify their physiological actions as well as to understand their impact on conformational changes in the channel molecule.
evidence: This is stated as an argument based on the findings.
